source: MET is a RTK expressed mainly in epithelial cells and activated by its high-affinity ligand, hepatocyte growth factor (HGF).

source: MET activation by HGF promotes a program known as invasive growth, comprising cell division, cell motility, extracellular matrix digestion, invasion, survival, and morphogenic differentiation (Bardelli et al., 1997a; Tamagnone and Comoglio, 1997; Rubin et al., 1993).

claim: The MET/HGF pair is involved in embryonic development.

claim: The MET/HGF pair is involved in development of specific organs/tissues such as the placenta, liver, lung, and muscle.

source: MET is synthesized as a precursor which matures through proteolytic cleavage.

source: This leads to the formation of a heterodimeric receptor composed of an extracellular part, containing a SEMA domain, a PSI domain, and four immunoglobulin plexin transcription factor (IPT) domains, and an intracellular part, containing a juxtamembrane domain (JM), a tyrosine kinase domain (TKD), and a C-terminal tail (Figure 1; Stella and Comoglio, 1999; Fernandes et al., 2019; Montagne et al., 2014).

claim: The extracellular part of MET contains a SEMA domain, a PSI domain, and four immunoglobulin plexin transcription factor (IPT) domains.
source: This leads to the formation of a heterodimeric receptor composed of an extracellular part, containing a SEMA domain, a PSI domain, and four immunoglobulin plexin transcription factor (IPT) domains, and an intracellular part, containing a juxtamembrane domain (JM), a tyrosine kinase domain (TKD), and a C-terminal tail (Figure 1; Stella and Comoglio, 1999; Fernandes et al., 2019; Montagne et al., 2014).

claim: The intracellular part of MET contains a juxtamembrane domain (JM), a tyrosine kinase domain (TKD), and a C-terminal tail.
source: This leads to the formation of a heterodimeric receptor composed of an extracellular part, containing a SEMA domain, a PSI domain, and four immunoglobulin plexin transcription factor (IPT) domains, and an intracellular part, containing a juxtamembrane domain (JM), a tyrosine kinase domain (TKD), and a C-terminal tail (Figure 1; Stella and Comoglio, 1999; Fernandes et al., 2019; Montagne et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the domain structure of the intracellular region, supported by Figure 1 and citations.

claim: HGF is a 90 kDa heterodimeric protein composed of an α subunit with an N domain and four loop domains (domains k1 to k4) and a β chain displaying homology to a serine protease domain (SPH) but lacking catalytic activity.
source: HGF, the high-affinity ligand of MET, is a 90 kDa heterodimeric protein composed of an α subunit with an N domain and four loop domains (domains k1 to k4) and a β chain displaying homology to a serine protease domain (SPH) but lacking catalytic activity (Gherardi et al., 2003).
evidence: This describes the structure of HGF, supported by a citation.

claim: The HGF/MET interaction is ensured by binding the SPH and k1 domains of HGF to the SEMA domain of MET.
source: The HGF/MET interaction is ensured by binding the SPH and k1 domains of HGF to the SEMA domain of MET (Gherardi et al., 2006; Uchikawa et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the molecular interaction between HGF and MET, supported by citations.

claim: MET dimerization could be ensured by HGF dimerization via a top-to-tail interaction of N and k1, leading to a 2:2 symmetric HGF/MET structure.
source: First, MET dimerization could be ensured by HGF dimerization via a top-to-tail interaction of N and k1. This would lead to the association of two MET receptors, each interacting with an HGF. This 2:2 model of interaction suggests a symmetric HGF/MET structure (Gherardi et al., 2006).
evidence: This describes one proposed model of MET dimerization, supported by a citation.

claim: One HGF can bind two MET receptors, one through the SPH domain and one through the k1 domain, leading to an asymmetric 2:1 model of MET dimerization.
source: Second, in a recent study, it has been proposed that one HGF can bind two MET receptors, one through the SPH domain and one through the k1 domain, this leading to MET dimerization. This asymmetric 2:1 model could be further stabilized by heparin and/or binding of a second HGF to the second MET receptor (Uchikawa et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes an alternative model of MET dimerization, supported by a recent citation.

claim: Upon HGF binding, MET undergoes phosphorylation on two residues of the catalytic domain (Y1252/Y1253 or Y1234/Y1235 in the short MET isoform).
source: Once the MET receptor interacts with its ligand, it undergoes phosphorylation on two residues of the catalytic domain (Y1252/Y1253 or Y1234/Y1235 in the short MET isoform).
evidence: This describes the initial phosphorylation event upon MET activation.

claim: After initial phosphorylation, other MET residues outside the catalytic domain are phosphorylated, including residue Y1367/Y1374 (Y1349/Y1356 in the short isoform) in the C-terminal tail.
source: Subsequently, other residues outside the catalytic domain are phosphorylated, including residue Y1367/Y1374 (Y1349/Y1356 in the short isoform) in the C-terminal tail, called the multi-substrate docking site (Longati et al., 1994; Ponzetto et al., 1994)
evidence: This describes subsequent phosphorylation events, supported by citations.

claim: Phosphorylated tyrosines in the C-terminal tail of MET are able to recruit multiple effectors such as GAB1, GRB2, SHC, PI3K, SRC, STAT3, and PLCγ.
source: as phosphorylated tyrosines in the C-terminal tail are able to recruit multiple effectors such as GRB2-associated binder-1 (GAB1), growth factor receptor–bound protein-2 (GRB2), SRC homology 2 domain-containing (SHC), phosphoinositide 3 kinase (PI3K), non-receptor tyrosine kinase SRC, signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3), and phospholipase C-gamma (PLCγ).
evidence: This describes the signaling molecules recruited to activated MET.

claim: The multisubstrate docking site of MET plays a key role in the induction of intracellular signalling pathways and biological responses including survival, motility, invasion, and cell cycle progression.
source: This multisubstrate docking site plays a key role in the induction by MET of intracellular signalling pathways and biological responses including survival, motility, invasion, and cell cycle progression (Figure 1; Ponzetto et al., 1993; Chiara et al., 2003; Rhoades Smith and Bilen, 2019).
evidence: This describes the functional importance of the docking site, supported by citations and Figure 1.

claim: MET signalling is downregulated by the juxtamembrane region of the cytoplasmic part of the receptor, encoded by exon 14 with its phosphorylated Tyr1021.
source: In parallel, MET signalling is downregulated by the juxtamembrane region of the cytoplasmic part of the receptor, encoded by exon 14 with its phosphorylated Tyr1021 (Tyr1003 in the short MET isoform) (Cortot et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes a negative regulatory mechanism, supported by a citation.

claim: MET gene amplification or copy number gain (CNG), leading to MET overexpression and its ligand-independent activation, has been identified as responsible for carcinogenesis in several tumour types including glioblastoma.
source: First, MET gene amplification or copy number gain (CNG), leading to MET overexpression and its ligand-independent activation, has been identified as responsible for carcinogenesis in several tumour types including glioblastoma (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2023)
evidence: This describes one mechanism of MET activation in cancer, supported by a citation.

claim: MET gene amplification or copy number gain has been identified as responsible for carcinogenesis in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD).
source: First, MET gene amplification or copy number gain (CNG), leading to MET overexpression and its ligand-independent activation, has been identified as responsible for carcinogenesis in several tumour types including glioblastoma (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2023), lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) (Collisson et al., 2014)
evidence: This describes MET amplification in LUAD, supported by a citation.

claim: MET gene amplification or copy number gain has been identified as responsible for carcinogenesis in gastric cancer (GC).
source: gastric cancer (GC) (Asaoka et al., 2010)
evidence: This describes MET amplification in gastric cancer, supported by a citation.

claim: MET gene amplification or copy number gain has been identified as responsible for carcinogenesis in colorectal cancer (CRC).
source: colorectal cancer (CRC) (Umeki et al., 1999)

claim: MET gene amplification or copy number gain has been identified as responsible for carcinogenesis in medulloblastoma.
source: and medulloblastoma (Tong et al., 2004).

claim: MET overexpression caused by gene amplification was first observed in gastric carcinoma, where it led to MET activation and transformation of several cell lines.
source: The phenomenon was observed for the first time in gastric carcinoma, where MET overexpression caused by gene amplification led to its activation and to the transformation of several cell lines (Ponzetto et al., 1991).
evidence: This is a historical claim about the first observation of MET amplification, supported by a citation.

claim: HGF overexpression has been observed in breast, gastric, colon, and lung cancers and leads to aberrant MET activation through establishment of an autocrine loop.
source: Second, HGF overexpression has been observed in breast, gastric, colon, and lung cancers and leads to aberrant MET activation through establishment of an autocrine loop (Ujiie et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes another mechanism of MET activation in cancer, supported by a citation.

claim: Chromosomal rearrangement leading to MET fusion with another gene is found in a limited number of tumours and leads to constitutive MET activation or overexpression.
source: The third mechanism, found in a limited number of tumours, is chromosomal rearrangement leading to MET fusion with another gene. This leads notably to constitutive MET activation or overexpression and involves fusions including KIF5B-MET in LUAD and BAIAP2L1-MET and C8ORF34-MET in RCC (Stransky et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes MET fusion events in cancer, supported by a citation.

claim: KIF5B-MET fusion occurs in LUAD.
source: This leads notably to constitutive MET activation or overexpression and involves fusions including KIF5B-MET in LUAD and BAIAP2L1-MET and C8ORF34-MET in RCC (Stransky et al., 2014).
evidence: This identifies a specific fusion in LUAD, supported by a citation.

claim: BAIAP2L1-MET and C8ORF34-MET fusions occur in RCC.
source: This leads notably to constitutive MET activation or overexpression and involves fusions including KIF5B-MET in LUAD and BAIAP2L1-MET and C8ORF34-MET in RCC (Stransky et al., 2014).
evidence: This identifies specific fusions in RCC, supported by a citation.

claim: The majority of MET mutations were found in papillary renal cancer and are located in the tyrosine kinase domain of MET.
source: The majority of MET mutations were found in papillary renal cancer and are located in the tyrosine kinase domain of MET.
evidence: This summarizes the distribution of MET mutations by cancer type and location.

claim: Over the last decade, MET mutations have been identified outside the kinase domain.
source: Over the last decade, however, other mutations have been identified outside the kinase domain.
evidence: This is a temporal claim about the discovery of non-kinase domain mutations.

claim: In NSCLC, missense mutations have been found in the SEMA and JM domains, in addition to mutations leading to exon 14 skipping.
source: In NSCLC, for instance, missense mutations have been found in the SEMA and JM domains, in addition to a large panel of mutations leading to exon 14 skipping (Tovar and Graveel, 2017; Ma et al., 2005; Ma et al., 2003; Krishnaswamy et al., 2009; Schrock et al., 2016; Figure 1 and Table 1).

claim: More than 160 different alterations affecting MET exon 14 have been described.
source: Since then, more than 160 different alterations affecting MET exon 14 have been described, including point mutations, deletions, insertions, and complex mutations (indels) which all affect conserved sequences of donor or acceptor splice sites (Figure 2A; Schrock et al., 2016).

source: Renal cell carcinoma is the most common type of kidney cancer in adults.

claim: Schmidt et al. found HPRC to segregate with a locus on chromosome 7q, carrying the MET proto-oncogene.

claim: Chromosome-7 duplication, rather than loss at this location, suggested the involvement of an oncogene suspected of being MET.
source: Chromosome-7 duplication, rather than the loss at this location, suggested the involvement of an oncogene suspected of being MET (Schmidt et al., 1997).

claim: Through analysis of nine families affected by papillary renal carcinoma and sporadic papillary renal carcinoma, missense mutations of MET were identified, all located in the kinase domain.
source: Through analysis of nine families affected by papillary renal carcinoma and sporadic papillary renal carcinoma, missense mutations of MET were identified, all located in the kinase domain, among which germline mutations (M1149T, V1206L, V1238I, D1246N, and Y1248C) and somatic mutations (D1246H, Y1228C, and M1268T) (Schmidt et al., 1997; Schmidt et al., 1999).

claim: Germline MET mutations identified in papillary renal carcinoma include M1149T, V1206L, V1238I, D1246N, and Y1248C.
source: Through analysis of nine families affected by papillary renal carcinoma and sporadic papillary renal carcinoma, missense mutations of MET were identified, all located in the kinase domain, among which germline mutations (M1149T, V1206L, V1238I, D1246N, and Y1248C) and somatic mutations (D1246H, Y1228C, and M1268T) (Schmidt et al., 1997; Schmidt et al., 1999).

evidence: This lists specific somatic mutations, supported by citations.

source: Biochemical and biological assays on murine fibroblasts transfected with MET cDNA demonstrated an increase in MET autophosphorylation when mutations were inserted, demonstrating that these are able to cause constitutive activity of the MET receptor (Tovar and Graveel, 2017; Bardelli et al., 1997b; Jeffers et al., 1997; Bardelli et al., 1998; Graveel et al., 2004; Michieli et al., 1999).

claim: MET mutations are able to cause constitutive activity of the MET receptor.

source: Next, analysis of focus formation, cell motility, and tumour growth in athymic mice demonstrated a correlation between MET enzymatic activity and the transforming properties of the different mutants (Bardelli et al., 1997a; Schmidt et al., 1997; Bardelli et al., 1998; Graveel et al., 2004).

source: The two most strongly activating variants, M1268T and Y1248H, displayed constitutive activity, being found to transform fibroblasts even in the absence of HGF (Michieli et al., 1999).

claim: Other evaluated MET mutations (M1149T, V1206L, L1213V, V1238I), displaying weaker activity, still required HGF stimulation for enhanced MET receptor phosphorylation and cell transformation.

claim: Activating MET mutations play a key role in promoting tumorigenesis.
source: This provides strong evidence that activating MET mutations play a key role in promoting tumorigenesis (Graveel et al., 2004; Graveel et al., 2005).

source: These data are also in agreement with the view that a conformational change induced by a particular mutation in the kinase domain may interfere with the binding of particular MET TKIs. For instance, the resistance mutations at positions 1181 and 1248 are consistent with steric hindrance of crizotinib binding (crizotinib being a type I TKI) (Figure 3B; Figure 3—video 1)
evidence: This describes the structural basis of resistance, supported by Figure 3B.

claim: The resistance mutations at positions 1213 and 1218 are consistent with steric hindrance of merestinib binding.
source: while the resistance mutations at positions 1213 and 1218 are consistent with steric hindrance merestinib binding, the latter being a type II TKI (Figure 3B; Figure 3—video 2).
evidence: This describes the structural basis of resistance, supported by Figure 3B.

claim: MET variants with resistance mutations against type I TKIs appear to be sensitive to type II inhibitors, and vice versa.
source: Interestingly, MET variants with resistance mutations against type I TKIs appear to be sensitive to type II inhibitors, and vice versa (Fujino et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes a strategy to overcome resistance, supported by a citation.

claim: Resistance might be overcome through the complementary activity of different MET TKIs.
source: This suggests that resistance might be overcome through the complementary activity of different MET TKIs.
evidence: This is an inference about therapeutic strategy.

claim: Expression of a MET variant displaying both exon 14 skipping and a D1246N or Y1248C mutation drives resistance to type I but not type II inhibitors in NIH3T3 cells.
source: Similar results have been obtained on NIH3T3 cells: expression of a MET variant displaying both exon 14 skipping and a D1246N or Y1248C mutation was found to drive resistance to type I but not type II inhibitors (Engstrom et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes cell model results, supported by a citation.

claim: A patient with a MET exon 14 skipping mutation who displayed resistance to crizotinib had additional MET mutations: D1246N, Y1248H/S, and G1181R.
source: In the same publication, the authors report a patient with a MET exon 14 skipping mutation who displayed resistance to crizotinib, associated with the presence of the following additional MET mutations: D1246N, Y1248H/S, and G1181R.
evidence: This describes a clinical case, implicitly supported by the Engstrom et al. reference.

claim: Treatment switch from the type I inhibitor crizotinib to the type II inhibitor glesatinib led to the regression of some metastatic localizations, with disappearance of the Y1248H/S mutation.
source: On the basis of results obtained on cell models, treatment was switched from the type I inhibitor crizotinib to the type II inhibitor glesatinib. This led to the regression of some metastatic localizations, with disappearance of the Y1248H/S mutation.
evidence: This describes a clinical response to treatment switch.

claim: Disappearance of the Y1248H/S mutation after switching to glesatinib was concomitant with the appearance of an L1213V mutation.
source: This disappearance was concomitant, however, with the appearance of an L1213V mutation (Engstrom et al., 2017), identified in a study by Fujino et al., 2019 as leading to resistance to type II TKIs.
evidence: This describes the emergence of a new resistance mutation, supported by citations.

claim: A patient with an initial EGFR-activating mutation developed primary resistance to an EGFR TKI through MET amplification.
source: A case report describes a patient with an initial EGFR-activating mutation, who developed primary resistance to an EGFR TKI through MET amplification (Bahcall et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes a case of MET-mediated resistance to EGFR TKI, supported by a citation.

claim: Co-treatment with an EGFR TKI and the MET TKI savolitinib led to a dramatic positive clinical response in a patient with MET amplification.
source: Co-treatment with an EGFR TKI and the MET TKI savolitinib led to a dramatic positive clinical response, but after several months of co-treatment, the patient experienced a relapse associated with detection of an additional MET D1246V mutation, previously described as an activating mutation (Jeffers et al., 1997).
evidence: This describes a clinical response and subsequent resistance, supported by citations.

claim: The D1246V mutant is resistant to type I TKIs (including savolitinib), but not to type II MET inhibitors.
source: In the same study, interestingly, the authors demonstrated with reconstituted MET mutations in cell lines that the D1246V mutant is resistant to type I TKIs (including savolitinib), but not to type II MET inhibitors.
evidence: This describes the resistance profile of D1246V, implicitly supported by the Bahcall et al. reference.

claim: Treatment with an EGFR TKI and cabozantinib, a type II MET TKI, led to a very good response in progressive lung disease with D1246V mutation.
source: This finding led to adapting the treatment: the EGFR TKI was used with cabozantinib, a type II MET TKI. To this treatment, the progressive lung disease responded very well (Bahcall et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes a successful treatment adaptation, supported by a citation.

claim: In patients displaying MET gene amplification, treatments with various TKIs led to the appearance of potential resistance mutations, including substitutions at D1246 and Y1248.
source: In a recent study on patients displaying MET gene amplification (following or not treatment with EGFR TKI), treatments with various TKIs led to the appearance of potential resistance mutations, including substitutions at D1246 and Y1248. Interestingly, similar mutations have been found in the context of exon 14 skipping (Yao et al., 2023)
evidence: This describes resistance mutations in MET amplification context, supported by a citation.

claim: At least the main on-target resistances are common between the WT MET receptor and the METex14Del variant.
source: suggesting that at least the main on-target resistances are common between the WT MET receptor and the METex14Del variant.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of similar resistance mutations.

claim: MET mutations are viewed as drivers if functional data have demonstrated their ability to induce cell transformation and/or experimental tumour growth.
source: MET mutations are viewed as drivers if functional data have demonstrated their ability to induce cell transformation and/or experimental tumour growth.
evidence: This defines the criteria for classifying MET mutations as drivers.

claim: Several dozen different residues are known to be affected by amino acid substitutions leading to MET activation.
source: To date, several dozen different residues are known to be affected by amino acid substitutions leading to MET activation.
evidence: This quantifies the number of known activating mutations.

claim: MET mutations first found in the kinase domain were recorded mainly in renal cancers and lead to kinase domain activation and induction of downstream intracellular pathways contributing to cell transformation.
source: Such mutations were first found in the kinase domain and recorded mainly in renal cancers. They lead to kinase domain activation and to induction of downstream intracellular pathways contributing to cell transformation.
evidence: This summarizes the characteristics of kinase domain mutations.

claim: The vast majority of MET mutations recorded in lung cancer lead to exon 14 skipping.
source: The vast majority of MET mutations recorded in lung cancer, in contrast to renal cancer, lead to exon 14 skipping: about 160 different mutations having been recorded (; Ma et al., 2003; Schrock et al., 2016; Frampton et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This contrasts the mutation types between lung and renal cancer, supported by citations.

claim: The strict differential distribution of MET mutations among cancers (kinase domain for renal cancer and MET exon 14 for NSCLC) suggests that specific organ contexts favour specific transformation mechanisms.
source: Thus, although both types of mutation lead to MET receptor activation, their strict differential distribution among cancers (kinase domain for renal cancer and MET exon 14 for NSCLC) suggests that specific organ contexts favour specific transformation mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference about the relationship between organ context and mutation type.

claim: METex14Del, in contrast to kinase-domain-mutated MET variants, induces sustained downstream signalling, including RAS-ERK signalling, well known to be activated in lung cancer.
source: For example, it has been shown that METex14Del, in contrast to kinase-domain-mutated MET variants, induces sustained downstream signalling, including RAS-ERK signalling, well known to be activated in lung cancer.
evidence: This contrasts the signaling properties of different MET mutations.

claim: Exon 14 skipping leads to loss of the caspase regulatory site and hence to resistance to apoptosis, a property that could favour tumorigenesis in the lung.
source: In addition, exon 14 skipping leads to loss of the caspase regulatory site and hence to resistance to apoptosis, a property that could also favour tumorigenesis in the lung.
evidence: This describes a mechanism by which exon 14 skipping could promote tumorigenesis.

claim: The METex14Del variant requires HGF stimulation.
source: It is worth noting that the METex14Del variant requires HGF stimulation, in keeping with deletion of a regulatory domain (Fernandes et al., 2023a).
evidence: This describes the ligand dependence of METex14Del, supported by a citation.

claim: RTKs with activating mutations may still require ligand stimulation.
source: It thus seems that RTKs with activating mutations may still require ligand stimulation.
evidence: This is a generalization from the METex14Del observation.

claim: Most of the kinase-domain-mutated MET forms recorded in renal cancers can be further stimulated by HGF, with the exception of the form bearing the M1268T mutation.
source: Likewise, MET variants with activating mutations in the kinase domain could also require ligand stimulation to achieve full receptor activation, as suggested by numerous experimental observations demonstrating that most of the kinase-domain-mutated MET forms recorded in renal cancers can be further stimulated by HGF, with the exception of the form bearing the M1268T mutation (Chiara et al., 2003; Graveel et al., 2004; Michieli et al., 1999; Graveel et al., 2005).
evidence: This describes the ligand dependence of kinase domain mutations, supported by citations.

claim: HGF expression by tumour cells or by the tumour microenvironment could be an attractive biomarker for predicting MET activation and its sensitivity to targeted therapies, even in the context of MET mutation.
source: Consequently, HGF expression by tumour cells or by the tumour microenvironment could be an attractive biomarker for predicting MET activation and thus its sensitivity to targeted therapies, even in the context of MET mutation.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential biomarkers.

claim: Treating patients with MET TKIs has led to identifying a novel generation of MET-activating mutations able to cause resistance.
source: Recently, treating patients with MET TKIs has led to identifying a novel generation of MET-activating mutations able to cause resistance (Awad et al., 2018; Dong et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2019; Heist et al., 2016; Jin et al., 2019; Li et al., 2017; Ou et al., 2017; Recondo et al., 2020; Rotow et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the discovery of resistance mutations, supported by citations.

claim: Novel resistance mutations are located mainly near the interface between MET and its TKI, easily visible in 3D structures.
source: These novel mutations are located mainly near the interface between MET and its TKI, easily visible in 3D structures (Figure 3B), and lead to inhibition of TKI binding to its target.
evidence: This describes the structural location of resistance mutations, supported by Figure 3B.

claim: Novel resistance mutations lead to inhibition of TKI binding to its target.
source: These novel mutations are located mainly near the interface between MET and its TKI, easily visible in 3D structures (Figure 3B), and lead to inhibition of TKI binding to its target.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of resistance mutations.

claim: Some of the resistance mutations discovered are not novel, having already been identified in hereditary and sporadic renal cancer.
source: Interestingly, some of the resistance mutations discovered are not novel, having already been identified in hereditary and sporadic renal cancer.
evidence: This connects resistance mutations to previously known mutations.

claim: With the extensive use of high-throughput sequencing for molecular diagnosis and the recent use of targeted therapies against MET, novel MET mutations are constantly being discovered.
source: With the extensive use of high-throughput sequencing for molecular diagnosis, along with the recent use of targeted therapies against MET, novel MET mutations are thus constantly being discovered.
evidence: This describes the ongoing discovery of new mutations.

claim: The challenge is no longer to identify MET mutations but to characterize them functionally.
source: The challenge is no longer to identify MET mutations but to characterize them functionally, in order (1) to identify them as potential targets for therapy, (2) to adapt treatment in case of resistance, (3) to understand why specific classes of mutations are associated with specific cancer types, and (4) to identify novel biomarkers in order to improve targeting of mutated MET.
evidence: This is a statement about the current challenges in the field.
